source.title: CowClip: Reducing CTR Prediction Model Training Time from 12 hours to 10 minutes on 1 GPU
source.authors: Zangwei Zheng; Peng Xu; Xuan Zou; Da Tang; Zhen Li; Chen-Guang Xi; Peng Wu; Leqi Zou; Yijie Zhu; Ming-yue Chen; Xian-Zhu Ding; Fuzhao Xue; Zi-Heng Qin; You-Long Cheng; Yang You

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the effect of batch size on held-out performance in CTR prediction, extending the large-batch question to a different task and dataset domain.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test AUC and LogLoss by batch size and scaling method. It does not report a training-to-test error gap, and it does not test memorization of random labels. Its evidence bears on V5 through held-out performance under fixed 10-epoch training.
record.test_reason: The study tests V5 in a new setting: CTR prediction. It compares held-out AUC across batch sizes with a fixed 10-epoch budget, finding penalties with conventional recipes and substantial recovery with an adapted recipe.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors attribute conventional scaling failures to unequal id frequencies and report that CowClip with an adapted recipe preserves or improves final performance through 128K on Criteo and approximately 64K on Avazu. Recovery depends on scaling, warmup and initialization; they acknowledge losses at larger batches and at the first epoch. Applicability to NLP is proposed rather than experimentally demonstrated.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Adam with embedding L2 regularization and 10 epochs; compares conventional scaling rules and introduces CowClip, adaptive column-wise gradient clipping with a batch-size scaling rule. This study evaluates CTR recommendation models rather than the image and language benchmarks emphasized in V5.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, batch size, scaling method, and architecture change the reported held-out performance. The paper notes a small-batch first-epoch AUC drop at large batches, although final 10-epoch results are maintained with CowClip.
record.problems: The paper reports three random seeds and states AUC standard deviation is less than 0.012%, but most tabulated results do not give per-condition uncertainty. It evaluates final test performance rather than the training-to-test error gap directly.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the remaining batch-size cells and LogLoss entries in Tables 4, 5, 11, and 12, plus other dataset and architecture combinations in the appendices, to stay within 60 rows. The selected rows capture the conventional-scaling penalty, the Criteo 1K-to-128K comparison across architectures, and the Avazu 64K/128K qualification. All models use the stated 10-epoch training schedule.

untested.parts: Fitting random labels and comparing natural-label and random-label held-out performance.
Width scaling beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Held-out performance comparisons between adaptive optimizers and SGD under different tuning budgets.

Image classification and language modeling; recovery by longer training; controlled isolation of every component of the adapted recipe. The one-epoch observation is an intermediate checkpoint, not a separately optimized one-epoch training experiment.
No documented dropout comparison with configurations and results is supplied. The implementation section merely states that dropout did not improve performance.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Removing examples selected by label memorization and retraining.

missing.what: The frequency ablation changes scaling-rule success: after retaining three frequent ids per field and pooling the rest, 8K square-root and linear scaling each lose only 0.01 AUC percentage points, versus 0.21 and 0.20 on unmodified Criteo in this experiment. Keep this experiment distinct from Table 4.
missing.locator: Table 2; Failure cause of traditional scaling rules

missing.what: Recipe ablations show that successful scaling depends on dense-layer scaling and warmup. Linear dense scaling diverges; empirical scaling declines from 80.85 at 8K to 79.83 at 128K; removing warmup declines from 80.97 to 80.52.
The authors explicitly report AUC loss even with CowClip at batch sizes of 256K or larger, without tabulated values.
missing.locator: Discussion and Future Work, second limitation

missing.what: Large batches have lower first-epoch test AUC despite maintained or improved final performance; the authors say weaker L2 regularization is needed to maintain first-epoch AUC.
missing.locator: Figure 8; Discussion and Future Work, one-epoch training paragraph

record.verdict_notes: CTR prediction is a T3 extension of V5's batch-size question. An explicit training-to-test gap is unnecessary because V5 names held-out performance. Improved performance with an adapted recipe supports V5's recovery clause. The reversed row states describe increased AUC relative to the penalty direction; they do not challenge that qualified claim. Remaining table cells and LogLoss results are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Network width beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization comparisons.
Image-classification and language-model settings; large batches under alternative epoch budgets; the effect on the train-to-test gap itself.
Sharpness and other measured properties tracking the generalization gap.
